newsitem.title: USA: NY Fed's McDonough says U.S. expansion continuing.
newsitem.headline: NY Fed's McDonough says U.S. expansion continuing.

text.p: The U.S. economic expansion is continuing and shows few, if any, signs of abating, Federal Reserve Bank of New York President William McDonough said on Wednesday.

Speaking before the New Jersey Council on Economic Education here, McDonough said, "The national economic expansion, already one of the longest in the post-World War II era, is entering its sixth year and shows few, if any, signs of coming to an imminent conclusion."
McDonough added that he was "quite encouraged" by the recent performance of most key U.S. economic indicators, particularly the "continued good news on inflation."
"Consumer price inflation, while up slightly during the third quarter of this year, gives no indication that it will accelerate persistently over the months ahead," he said.

Retail-level inflation, measured by the government's Consumer Price Index (CPI) stood at an annual rate of 2.3 percent in the third quarter. The New York Fed chief pointed out CPI has increased by about 3.0 percent or less in each of the last five years, a record unequaled since the 1960s.
McDonough said at least some of the credit for the nation's favorable inflation performance belongs to the "forward-looking policies" of the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee.

McDonough said the Fed's pre-emptive strike against inflation in February 1994 was necessary because monetary policy works with long and uncertain lags. He said the effects of monetary policy on inflation take about three years.

"Thus it was clear to us in 1994, and it's just as clear today, that the failure to contain inflation at its earliest, incipient stages only makes it costlier and more time consuming to bring it under control later," McDonough said.
